body.en: When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, eight angles appear — but only two distinct measures. Knowing which pairs are equal and which are supplementary unlocks most angle-chase problems.
Corresponding angles are equal; alternate (interior or exterior) angles are equal; co-interior (same-side interior) angles are supplementary, summing to \( 180^{\circ} \).

Euclidean Invariants, Locus Equations & Scaling Laws: In analytic geometry, geometric loci translate into algebraic constraints via Euclidean distance \(d = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2}\). A circle of center \((h, k)\) and radius \(r\) satisfies \((x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2\), and a tangent line at point \(P\) is strictly perpendicular to the radius \(CP\) (\(m_{\text{tan}} \cdot m_{\text{rad}} = -1\)). Under a similarity scale factor \(k\), all linear lengths scale by \(k\), surface areas scale by \(k^2\), and volumes scale by \(k^3\).

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Lines & Angles)

body.en:
Why Inscribed Angles Equal Half the Central Angle & Circle Completion Works: Given \(x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0\), completing the square in \(x\) and \(y\) simultaneously yields:

\[ (x + g)^2 - g^2 + (y + f)^2 - f^2 + c = 0 \implies (x + g)^2 + (y + f)^2 = g^2 + f^2 - c \]

Thus the center is \((-g, -f)\) and the radius is \(r = \sqrt{g^2 + f^2 - c}\) (requiring \(g^2 + f^2 > c\)). In any circle, drawing diameter \(POQ\) splits an inscribed angle \(\angle APB\) into two isosceles triangles \(\triangle OAP\) and \(\triangle OBP\) (since \(OA = OB = OP = r\)); by the exterior angle theorem, \(\angle AOB = 2\angle APB\).

Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One interior angle is \( 72^{\circ} \). Find its alternate interior angle.

Alternate interior angles are equal:

\[ 72^{\circ}. \]

A co-interior angle measures \( 110^{\circ} \). Find the other co-interior angle.

\[ 180^{\circ}-110^{\circ}=70^{\circ}. \]

label.en: Common Pitfall — Conflating Alternate and Consecutive Angles

body.en: A frequent error on SAT and ACT geometry questions is equating consecutive (same-side) interior angles instead of setting their sum to \( 180^{\circ} \). Remember the letter shapes: Z-angles (alternate interior) are equal; F-angles (corresponding) are equal; but C-angles (consecutive interior) are supplementary.

Problem (Medium): Two parallel lines, \(p\) and \(q\), are intersected by a transversal line \(t\). A pair of consecutive interior angles have measures \((4x + 9)^\circ\) and \((2x + 33)^\circ\). What is the value of \(x\)?

Step-by-Step Solution: By the Consecutive Interior Angles Theorem, when two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, consecutive interior angles are supplementary (their measures sum to \(180^\circ\)). Set up the equation: \[(4x + 9) + (2x + 33) = 180\] Combine like terms: \[6x + 42 = 180\] Subtract \(42\) from both sides: \[6x = 138\] Divide by \(6\): \[x = 23\] Evaluating the angle measures at \(x = 23\) gives \(4(23) + 9 = 101^\circ\) and \(2(23) + 33 = 79^\circ\), which are supplementary (\(101^\circ + 79^\circ = 180^\circ\)). Common Misconceptions: - Choice A (\(8\)): Mistakenly assumes consecutive interior angles are complementary, solving \(6x + 42 = 90\). - Choice B (\(12\)): Confuses consecutive interior angles with alternate interior angles and sets them equal, solving \(4x + 9 = 2x + 33\). - Choice D (\(37\)): Makes an algebraic sign error by adding \(42\) to \(180\) instead of subtracting, solving \(6x = 222\).

Problem (Hard): In a plane, two horizontal lines \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) are parallel, with \(\ell_1\) positioned above \(\ell_2\). A zig-zag transversal path connects point \(A\) on \(\ell_1\) to point \(D\) on \(\ell_2\) through intermediate vertices \(B\) and \(C\), which lie strictly between the two parallel lines. - Segment \(AB\) extends downward and to the right from \(A\), forming an acute angle of \(65^\circ\) with line \(\ell_1\). - Segment \(BC\) extends downward and to the left from \(B\) to \(C\). - Segment \(CD\) extends downward and to the right from \(C\), meeting line \(\ell_2\) at an acute angle of \(25^\circ\). If the ray that bisects \(\angle BCD\) is perpendicular to segment \(AB\), what is the measure of \(\angle ABC\)?

Step-by-Step Solution: To solve this crook-angle transversal problem, we construct auxiliary horizontal lines parallel to \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) through vertices \(B\) and \(C\). 1. **Determine the direction of the angle bisector of \(\angle BCD\):** - Segment \(AB\) slopes downward and to the right at an angle of \(65^\circ\) below the horizontal (direction angle \(-65^\circ\)). - Since the ray bisecting \(\angle BCD\) points into the interior of \(\angle BCD\) (to the right) and is perpendicular to segment \(AB\), its inclination angle relative to the horizontal is \(-65^\circ + 90^\circ = +25^\circ\) (i.e., \(25^\circ\) above the horizontal). 2. **Determine the direction of ray \(CB\):** - Construct an auxiliary horizontal line through vertex \(C\). - By alternate interior angles with \(\ell_2\), segment \(CD\) points downward and to the right at an angle of \(25^\circ\) below the horizontal (direction angle \(-25^\circ\)). - The angle between ray \(CD\) and the bisector ray is \(25^\circ - (-25^\circ) = 50^\circ\). - Because the ray bisects \(\angle BCD\), the angle between the bisector ray and ray \(CB\) is also \(50^\circ\). - Thus, ray \(CB\) points upward and to the right at an angle of \(25^\circ + 50^\circ = 75^\circ\) above the horizontal. 3. **Calculate \(m\angle ABC\) using the auxiliary horizontal line at \(B\):** - Through vertex \(B\), draw a horizontal line parallel to \(\ell_1\). - Segment \(BA\) extends upward and to the left, making an angle of \(65^\circ\) above the leftward horizontal ray (alternate interior to the \(65^\circ\) angle at \(A\)). - Segment \(BC\) extends downward and to the left, making an angle of \(75^\circ\) below the leftward horizontal ray (alternate interior to the \(75^\circ\) angle made by ray \(CB\) with the horizontal at \(C\)). - Summing these two adjacent angles gives: \[ m\angle ABC = 65^\circ + 75^\circ = 140^\circ \]

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Lines & Angles)

rows.en: Reading radius of \((x-3)^2 + (y+7)^2 = 16\) as \(r = 16\) or center as \((-3, 7)\)
Confuses \(r^2\) with \(r\) and forgets to flip the signs inside \((x-h)\) and \((y-k)\).
Take the square root and negate the constants: center \((3, -7)\), radius \(r = \sqrt{16} = 4\).
Using SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) to claim triangle congruence
The ambiguous case of the Sine Rule allows two distinct triangles (\(\theta\) and \(180^\circ - \theta\)).
Use valid congruence criteria only: SSS, SAS (included angle), ASA, AAS, or HL/RHS.
Cubing the area ratio \((A_1/A_2)^3\) to find the volume ratio of similar solids
Area ratio is already \(k^2\), so cubing it gives \(k^6\) instead of \(k^3\).
First take the square root to get linear scale factor \(k = \sqrt{A_1/A_2}\), then cube \(k^3\).

body.en: Geometric Auxiliary-Line Strategy (Honors Euclidean & Analytic Geometry): Whenever a circle problem includes a tangent line, draw the radius to the point of tangency and mark \(90^\circ\) immediately; whenever it includes a chord, drop the perpendicular bisector from the center to form a right triangle.

question.en: Two parallel lines are intersected by a transversal line. Two consecutive interior angles have measures \( (3x - 10)^{\circ} \) and \( (2x + 25)^{\circ} \). Find the measure of the acute angle.

solution.en:
Solution: Consecutive interior angles are supplementary, so they sum to \( 180^{\circ} \):

\[ (3x - 10) + (2x + 25) = 180 \implies 5x + 15 = 180 \implies 5x = 165 \implies x = 33. \]

Substitute \( x = 33 \) into both angle expressions:

\[ 3(33) - 10 = 89^{\circ}, \quad 2(33) + 25 = 91^{\circ}. \]

The acute angle has measure \( 89^{\circ} \).

hints.en: Solution: Consecutive interior angles are supplementary, so they sum to \( 180^{\circ} \): \((3x - 10) + (2x + 25) = 180 \implies 5x + 15 = 180 \implies 5x = 165 \implies x\).
Substitute \( x = 33 \) into both angle expressions: \(3(33) - 10 = 89^{\circ}, \quad 2(33) + 25 = 91^{\circ}\).

question.en: Two parallel lines \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) are cut by a transversal \(T\). A pair of alternate exterior angles are given by \((7x - 14)^{\circ}\) and \((4x + 31)^{\circ}\). Find the value of \(x\) and the measure of each alternate exterior angle.

solution.en:
Step 1: Set up the equation using alternate exterior angles: Alternate exterior angles created by parallel lines are congruent:

\[ 7x - 14 = 4x + 31 \implies 3x = 45 \implies x = 15. \]

Step 2: Evaluate the angle measure:

\[ 7(15) - 14 = 105 - 14 = 91^{\circ}. \]

Check: \(4(15) + 31 = 60 + 31 = 91^{\circ}\). Both alternate exterior angles measure \(91^{\circ}\).

hints.en: Set up the equation using alternate exterior angles: Alternate exterior angles created by parallel lines are congruent: \(7x - 14 = 4x + 31 \implies 3x = 45 \implies x\).
Check: \(4(15) + 31 = 60 + 31 = 91^{\circ}\). Both alternate exterior angles measure \(91^{\circ}\).

question.en: [Practice 3 · Easy] Two angles form a linear pair. The measures of the angles are \((3x + 10)^\circ\) and \((2x + 20)^\circ\). What is the value of \(x\)?

hints.en: By definition, two angles that form a linear pair are adjacent and supplementary, meaning the sum of their measures is equal to \(180^\circ\).
Set up the algebraic equation: \( (3x + 10) + (2x + 20) = 180 \) Combine like terms: \( 5x + 30 = 180 \) Subtract 30 from both sides: \( 5x = 150 \).
Divide both sides by 5 to determine \(x\).

solution.en:
By definition, two angles that form a linear pair are adjacent and supplementary, meaning the sum of their measures is equal to \(180^\circ\).

Set up the algebraic equation:
\( (3x + 10) + (2x + 20) = 180 \)

Combine like terms:
\( 5x + 30 = 180 \)

Subtract 30 from both sides:
\( 5x = 150 \)

Divide both sides by 5:
\( x = 30 \)

Analysis of incorrect choices:
- Choice A (10): Results from setting the two expressions equal to each other (\(3x + 10 = 2x + 20\)), confusing a linear pair with vertical angles.
- Choice B (12): Results from setting the sum equal to \(90^\circ\) instead of \(180^\circ\) (\(5x + 30 = 90\)), confusing supplementary angles with complementary angles.
- Choice D (100): Results from solving for the measure of the larger angle, \(3(30) + 10 = 100^\circ\), rather than the value of \(x\).

question.en: [Practice 4 · Medium] In the diagram below, lines \(m\) and \(n\) are parallel. A transversal line intersects \(m\) and \(n\). Another line segment connects a point on \(m\) to a point on \(n\), forming a "crook-angle". Given that \(\angle 1 = 120^\circ\) and \(\angle 2 = 135^\circ\), what is the measure of the "crook-angle" \(\angle 3\)?

hints.en: To solve this problem, we construct an auxiliary line through the vertex of \(\angle 3\) that is parallel to lines \(m\) and \(n\). Let's call this auxiliary line \(p\). This construction divides \(\angle 3\) into two angles, let's call them \(\angle 3a\) and \(\angle 3b\), such that \(\angle 3 = \angle 3a + \angle 3b\).

Now consider line \(n\) parallel to line \(p\). The transversal that forms \(\angle 2\) intersects both \(n\) and \(p\). The angle supplementary to \(\angle 2\) is \(180^\circ - 135^\circ = 45^\circ\). This \(45^\circ\) angle and \(\angle 3b\) are alternate interior angles with respect to the transversal and parallel lines \(n\) and \(p\). Therefore, \(\angle 3b = 45^\circ\).
The total "crook-angle" \(\angle 3\) is the sum of \(\angle 3a\) and \(\angle 3b\). So, \(\angle 3 = \angle 3a + \angle 3b = 60^\circ + 45^\circ\).

solution.en:
To solve this problem, we construct an auxiliary line through the vertex of \(\angle 3\) that is parallel to lines \(m\) and \(n\). Let's call this auxiliary line \(p\). This construction divides \(\angle 3\) into two angles, let's call them \(\angle 3a\) and \(\angle 3b\), such that \(\angle 3 = \angle 3a + \angle 3b\). 

Since line \(m\) is parallel to line \(p\), and the transversal that forms \(\angle 1\) intersects both \(m\) and \(p\), \(\angle 1\) and \(\angle 3a\) are consecutive interior angles if we extend the transversal line. However, a more direct approach is to consider the relationship with \(\angle 1\). The angle supplementary to \(\angle 1\) is \(180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ\). This \(60^\circ\) angle and \(\angle 3a\) are alternate interior angles with respect to the transversal and parallel lines \(m\) and \(p\). Therefore, \(\angle 3a = 60^\circ\). 

Now consider line \(n\) parallel to line \(p\). The transversal that forms \(\angle 2\) intersects both \(n\) and \(p\). The angle supplementary to \(\angle 2\) is \(180^\circ - 135^\circ = 45^\circ\). This \(45^\circ\) angle and \(\angle 3b\) are alternate interior angles with respect to the transversal and parallel lines \(n\) and \(p\). Therefore, \(\angle 3b = 45^\circ\). 

The total "crook-angle" \(\angle 3\) is the sum of \(\angle 3a\) and \(\angle 3b\). So, \(\angle 3 = \angle 3a + \angle 3b = 60^\circ + 45^\circ = 105^\circ\).
